newsitem.title: UK: London's bourse poised for new order-drive trading.
newsitem.headline: London's bourse poised for new order-drive trading.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange, whose technology is still years behind that employed by other major world bourses, is gearing up for its biggest transition ever in 1997 with the introduction of electronic order-driven trading.
Not since the "Big Bang" market liberalisation of 10 years ago has London faced the prospect of such radical change.
"It's Big Bang time again," said Mike Jones, technical services director at Capel Cure Myers who's preparing his brokerage for order-driven trading.

"I think the order book will have a much bigger impact than Big Bang. Ten years ago, they took business off the trading floors and on to screens, but the order-driven system will fundamentally change the way the market operates," he added.
Order-driven dealing will be used to automatically match buyers and sellers in Britain's top 100 stocks, replacing the current system where market makers set the prices.
The new system, said one veteran of the industry, will result in a sharp reduction in all middlemen, especially agency dealers and market makers. And that means lower dealing costs.

"Prices are too wide at the moment because it is the risk-takers who fund the deal," he said. "The order book will bring prices closer together, cut costs and make the market more transparent. That will bring little benefit to the average investor. It will be a big benefit to the big institutions."
The targeted launch date for the new system is 10 months away, but the industry is still wrangling over the rules.

Under the amendments published by the LSE earlier this month, market makers will be permitted to delay reporting large block deals, even though other investors have to reveal their transactions immediately.

The LSE defends the concessions, saying that allowing the delay help preserve market liquidity as market makers would be less willing to risk large capital if they were required to report big trades immediately.
"It's pragmatic," said one broker of the proposal. "There's no point in driving away business for purist ideals."
The industry has until January 10 to respond to the exchange's revised proposals.
The LSE said it will continue to fine-tune detailed rules, particularly for large trades, but said its proposals have received widespread market support.
The new arrangements, it said, "represent an evolutionary approach which should achieve at least this level and ensure both a high degree of transparency and a liquid order book."

Yet there has been much media speculation that regulator the Securities Investment Board (SIB) will demand changes to certain proposals. SIB spokesman Peter Parker said the reports were "total speculation," saying the agency "cannot take a final view until we see the finished package."
Meanwhile, CrestCo, the Bank of England-led group developing the electronic share settlement system for the LSE, is scheduled to complete the transition to a paperless regime by April 1997.

Crest -- born from the ruins of Taurus, the LSE's settlement system that ran up costs of some 38 million sterling ($64 million) before it was abandoned in 1993 -- was hailed as being on budget and on time only six months ago.
But since the inauguration of Crest in July, the system has experienced software and other problems, causing slow processing and huge backlogs of unmatched trades.
Currently, less than half of the FTSE 100 stocks are settled on Crest, and many settlement managers worry the system cannot cope with larger volumes. ($1=.5973 Sterling)
